config.title: @layer and cascade layers

intro.title: @layer and cascade layers
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage with multiple CSS rules to see how @layer and cascade layers control the priority of styles. You'll learn the core concept of CSS cascade layers, which allow you to organize and manage style precedence without relying on specificity or source order. The main technology involved is the CSS @layer at-rule, which you'll use to define named layers and apply styles within them. By the end, you'll understand how to create layers, assign styles to them, and predict which styles win when layers conflict, giving you a powerful tool for managing complex stylesheets.
intro.usecase: In real-world applications, CSS cascade layers are essential for managing complex style systems, such as design systems or component libraries. For example, a dashboard might use `@layer` to separate base styles (like resets), vendor styles (from third-party libraries), and custom component styles, ensuring predictable overrides. This pattern prevents specificity wars when integrating UI kits, theming engines, or modular panels, allowing developers to maintain clean, maintainable code in large-scale projects like admin interfaces or data visualization tools.

objectives: Construct a CSS stylesheet that defines multiple cascade layers using the @layer rule.
Apply styles within specific layers to control their cascade priority.
Manipulate the order of layers to determine which styles take precedence.
Integrate unlayered styles with layered styles and predict the outcome.
Configure a layer to import external styles and manage their cascade position.
Initialize a base layer for default styles and subsequent layers for overrides.
Implement a layer hierarchy to resolve style conflicts in a structured manner.

steps.title: Create a basic HTML structure with conflicting styles
steps.instruction: Create a simple HTML structure with multiple elements and conflicting CSS rules to demonstrate why cascade layers are needed.
steps.hint: Start by writing HTML elements like headings, paragraphs, and buttons. Then add CSS rules that target the same elements with different styles to create conflicts.

steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an HTML page with elements that have conflicting CSS rules applied, showing the lesson that cascade layers solve.
successCriteria: The code includes multiple HTML elements and at least two CSS rules that target the same element with conflicting property values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have at least two CSS rules that conflict for the same element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. Remember to create both HTML elements and CSS rules that conflict with each other.

steps.title: Introduce the @layer at-rule syntax
steps.instruction: Add a CSS @layer at-rule to declare your first cascade layer named 'base'.
steps.hint: Use the @layer syntax followed by a layer name to create a new cascade layer.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Similar: declaring a cascade layer */
@layer utilities;
steps.seedCode:
/* Add your HTML structure and conflicting CSS rules here */

@layer base;
steps.expectedOutcome: A cascade layer named 'base' is declared using the @layer at-rule.
successCriteria: The code contains '@layer base;' to declare the base cascade layer.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the exact syntax '@layer base;' to declare the layer.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to declare a cascade layer named 'base' using the @layer at-rule.

steps.title: Add styles to your first layer
steps.instruction: Inside your declared @layer base, add a CSS rule that sets the color of all paragraphs to blue.
steps.hint: After @layer base, add opening and closing curly braces, then write a rule like p { color: blue; } inside them.
steps.expectedOutcome: The @layer base now contains a rule that makes all paragraphs blue.
successCriteria: A CSS rule p { color: blue; } is placed inside @layer base {}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the rule inside the @layer base block with proper curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've placed the paragraph styling rule inside @layer base {} with the correct syntax.

steps.title: Create multiple layers with different names
steps.instruction: Declare two additional cascade layers named 'components' and 'utilities' after your existing 'base' layer declaration.
steps.hint: Use the @layer at-rule with the layer names separated by commas. For example: @layer components, utilities;
steps.analogousExample:
/* Declaring multiple layers */
@layer header, footer, sidebar;
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have three cascade layers declared: base, components, and utilities.
successCriteria: The code contains @layer base, components, utilities; or separate @layer declarations for components and utilities.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've declared both 'components' and 'utilities' layers. Check that you used the correct @layer syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: declare two additional cascade layers named 'components' and 'utilities' using the @layer at-rule.

steps.title: Define layer order by declaration
steps.instruction: Declare your three layers (base, components, utilities) in a specific order: first 'base',
steps.hint: Write three @layer declarations in sequence: @layer base; @layer components; @layer utilities;
steps.expectedOutcome: The layer order is established by declaration sequence, with later-declared layers taking precedence.
successCriteria: Three @layer declarations appear in the order: base, components, utilities.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You declared some layers, but not all three in the correct order. Make sure you have exactly: @layer base; @layer components; @layer utilities;
steps.feedbackWrong: The layer declarations are missing or incorrect. You need to declare three layers in this specific order: base, components, utilities.

steps.title: 'components', then 'utilities'
steps.hint: Write three @layer declarations in sequence: @layer base; @layer components; @layer utilities;

steps.title: Use the layer() function for imported styles
steps.instruction: Add an @import rule that uses the layer() function to import a hypothetical external stylesheet into your 'base' layer.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Example: importing external styles into a specific layer */
@import url('reset.css') layer(reset);
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have an @import rule that assigns external styles to your 'base' layer using the layer() function.
successCriteria: The code includes @import url('external.css') layer(base); or similar with correct syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the correct syntax: @import url('external.css') layer(base);
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to use @import with the layer() function to assign the imported styles to a specific layer.

steps.title: Create anonymous layers
steps.instruction: Declare an anonymous cascade layer using @layer without a name and add a CSS rule that sets the background color of all div elements to lightblue.
steps.hint: Use @layer { } without specifying a layer name. Inside the braces, write a CSS rule for div elements.
steps.expectedOutcome: An anonymous cascade layer is created with a rule that styles div elements.
successCriteria: The code contains @layer { div { background-color: lightblue; } } or equivalent anonymous layer declaration with a div rule.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using @layer { } without a name and including a CSS rule for div elements inside the braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: anonymous layers use @layer { } (no name after @layer). Inside, write div { background-color: lightblue; }.

steps.title: Establish explicit layer ordering
steps.instruction: Add explicit layer ordering by using @layer with the three layer names you declared earlier, in the order you want them to have precedence.
steps.hint: Use @layer followed by the layer names separated by commas, like @layer layer1, layer2, layer3;. This defines their order before any styles are added.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Example: defining layer order explicitly */
@layer utilities, components, base;
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file will now have an explicit @layer declaration that establishes the precedence order of your three named layers.
successCriteria: An @layer rule with three layer names separated by commas is added to the CSS file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using @layer with the exact three layer names you declared earlier, separated by commas.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we're looking for. Remember to use @layer followed by your three layer names in the order you want them to have precedence.

steps.title: Understand layer precedence rules
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph rule with high specificity (e.g., using an ID selector) inside your 'components' layer,
steps.hint: Use #special-paragraph { color: red; } in the components layer and p { color: blue; } in the base layer. The layer order should make the components layer win despite lower specificity.
steps.expectedOutcome: The learner will see that when layers are ordered (e.g., base, components), styles in later layers (components) override those in earlier layers (base) even if the earlier layer has higher specificity selectors.
successCriteria: Two paragraph rules exist: one with high specificity (ID selector) in the components layer, and one with normal specificity (element selector) in the base layer. The layer order is declared so components comes after base.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both paragraph rules: one with an ID selector in the components layer and one with just the element selector in the base layer. Also verify your layer order places components after base.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding two conflicting paragraph rules in different layers to show layer precedence. Check that you have: 1) A rule like #special-paragraph { color: red; } inside @layer components { ... }, and 2) A rule like p { color: blue; } inside @layer base { ... }, with layer order declared as base, components.

steps.title: Practice with a complete layer example
steps.instruction: Add a final example that demonstrates how cascade layers resolve conflicts: create a paragraph rule in the 'components' layer that sets color to blue, and another paragraph rule in the 'utilities' layer that sets color to red,
steps.hint: Add two CSS rules for the same paragraph element, each inside a different named layer. The layer declared later in the explicit ordering should win.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph will display red text because the 'utilities' layer (declared later in the explicit ordering) overrides the 'components' layer's blue color.
successCriteria: Two paragraph rules exist in different named layers ('components' and 'utilities') with conflicting color values, and the explicit layer ordering determines which color is applied.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have two paragraph rules in separate named layers (like 'components' and 'utilities') with different color values. The explicit layer order should determine the winner.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created two paragraph rules inside different named layers (e.g., @layer components and @layer utilities) with conflicting color values. The layer declared later in the explicit ordering should win.
